value: a 7 mT static magnetic field caused a significant increase in barley seed germination rate, accelerating root emergence, with root and shoot length and fresh biomass of the seedlings also stimulated
method: barley seeds on 1% agar without MS medium (condition B) in a coil giving 7 mT for 6 h a day over 5 days, against control seeds under the same conditions without the power supply; germination rate and seedling growth read at 5 days; t-test, three replicates
conditions: Calibration with a Hall-effect Gauss-meter; coil kept at 22 +/- 1 C, 14 h light 10 h dark, 60% humidity; three biological replicates with a minimum of 30 seeds per treatment (Figure 1 notes ten to twelve seedlings measured per experiment); the text prints no germination percentages (only Supplementary Figure 2E) and does not define the germination criterion; 7 mT is called the optimized treatment directly after the sentence 'Several MF flux densities and exposure times were examined (Shabrangi et al., 2010, 2011).', so the dose choice rests on the authors' earlier papers and no other flux density is tested in this one; the 1, 3 and 6 h exposures are in a supplementary figure only; the contrary result is on MS medium (condition A), where prolonged exposure to the field caused a decrease of seed germination rate and of growth characteristics, and short exposure there (7 mT for 6 h) caused growth inhibition 'which was less prominent than in long exposure'; the Methods name both a one-sample t-test and a Student t-test without explaining the difference; the quoted sentence cites Figures 1A-D, whose legend places them on agar without MS medium (condition B) at 7 mT for 6 h per day over 5 consecutive days, ten to twelve seedlings on average in three independent experiments, P <= 0.05

source.authors: Shabrangy A, Ghatak A, Zhang S, Priller A, Chaturvedi P, Weckwerth W
source.title: Magnetic Field Induced Changes in the Shoot and Root Proteome of Barley (Hordeum vulgare L.)

where: Results, first paragraph on seedling growth under magnetic field (Figure 1A-D)
quote: The optimized treatment was found to be 7 mT, which caused a significant increase in seed germination rate, accelerating the root emergence, with growth stimulation in the seedling including root and shoot length and fresh biomass of barley (Figures 1A–D).
note: Germination and seedling growth under an applied static field against an unpowered control; the paper reads it as a plant response to the field, and this record logs the germination and seedling-growth endpoints and no receptor is identified. Names: POWO page powo.science.kew.org/taxon/405391-1 says 'This species is accepted'; WFO page wfoplantlist.org/taxon/wfo-0000875054-2019-05 lists Hordeum vulgare as accepted (page flags an older snapshot). Licence sentence read on the publisher PDF: 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).' Search that reached the full text: 'Shabrangy 2021 Magnetic Fields Induce Barley Hordeum vulgare germination Frontiers in Plant Science static magnetic field 7 mT'. Control placement relative to the coil is not stated.

value: night warming during grain filling (FT) gave a similar spike number to the control but significantly lower grain number, 1,000-grain weight and yield (minus 17%)
method: field winter wheat under passive night warming (plastic membranes rolled down at dusk and up at dawn, about 19:00 to 07:00) applied after anthesis (FT), against an unwarmed control (CK); grain yield from Table 2, ANOVA with letters at p < 0.05
conditions: One growing season ('from 2013 to 2014', sown on October 26, 2013) at the Jiangpu Experimental Station of Nanjing Agricultural University; cultivars Yangmai 13 (vernal) and Yannong 19 (facultative); randomized block design, three replications, plots 8 m2; FT raised the mean night canopy temperature by 1.96 C, no daytime warming was tested; the quoted 17% is one overall figure (own arithmetic from Table 2 gives about 16.7% for Yangmai 13 and 17.4% for Yannong 19, not stated in the paper); Table 2 grain yield (kg hm-2) CK 7297.80 and FT 6079.67 for Yangmai 13, CK 6832.73 and FT 5645.86 for Yannong 19; the study is a priming design, so the other treatments (winter or spring night warming plus FT) raised yield above FT alone (WT + FT 6536.13 and ST + FT 6790.66 for Yangmai 13); the cultivar x treatment interaction was not significant; one warming facility (3 m by 5 m) is described and whether each block had its own is not stated; the membranes also change humidity and wind at night, which is not separated from temperature; Table 1 prints 'Yangmai 18' where the text says Yangmai 13

source.authors: Fan Y, Lv Z, Ge T, Li Y, Yang W, Zhang W, Ma S, Dai T, Huang Z
source.title: Night-Warming Priming at the Vegetative Stage Alleviates Damage to the Flag Leaf Caused by Post-anthesis Warming in Winter Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.)

quote: Compared with control, FT had a similar spike number but significantly lower grain number, 1,000-grain weight, and, therefore, yield (minus 17%).
note: Whole-plant field yield response to night warming after anthesis against an unwarmed control; this is a physiological endpoint and no thermoreceptor is identified. Names: POWO page powo.science.kew.org/taxon/332110-2 lists Triticum aestivum L. as accepted; WFO page wfoplantlist.org/taxon/wfo-0000905667-2023-06 lists Triticum aestivum (Linnaeus 1753) as accepted species (page flags an older snapshot). Licence sentence read on the publisher PDF: 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).' Search that reached the full text: 'Fan 2021 Triticum aestivum night warming free-air temperature increase yield Frontiers in Plant Science 12 706567'. Abstract gives the same direction: FT decreased yield by reducing the number of grains per panicle and 1,000-grain weight.

value: high temperature (30/25 C day/night) increased tomato seedling stem length and thickness and the number of xylem vessels compared with the control temperature (25/20 C)
method: tomato seedlings on rockwool blocks with liquid culture medium, 16 h photoperiod at 300 umol photons m-2 s-1, 7 days at 30/25 C (HT) or 25/20 C (CT) day/night, after 5 to 6 days pre-growth at 23/23 C; hypocotyl and epicotyl length and diameter (Figure 1B, C) and xylem number in hypocotyl cross-sections (Figure 1E) measured, Student t test
conditions: Cultivar Managua RZ; n = 7 seedlings per condition for stem length and diameter, n = 5 for xylem vessel counts, which cover hypocotyl cross-sections and only vessels wider than 50 um ('Number of xylems (diameter > 50 µm) in the cross section') (figure legend: *P < 0.01, **P < 0.001); the text prints no means; HT and CT share the same day-night difference (+5 C), so the contrast is absolute temperature, not DIF; the paper does not state the number of growth chambers or whether each temperature had replicate chambers, so chamber and temperature may be confounded; 'stem' is not defined in the text (hypocotyl and epicotyl were measured separately) and the Methods do not say how length and diameter were measured; the negative-DIF contrast (25/30 C) shortened stems but left thickness and xylem vessel number unchanged, and SlPIF4 expression was unaffected by DIF

source.authors: Ohtaka K, Yoshida A, Kakei Y, Fukui K, Kojima M, Takebayashi Y, Yano K, Imanishi S, Sakakibara H
source.title: Difference Between Day and Night Temperatures Affects Stem Elongation in Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) Seedlings via Regulation of Gibberellin and Auxin Synthesis

quote: Under positive DIF (when DT – NT > 0), in contrast to the control temperature (25°C/20°C, DT/NT), high temperature (30°C/25°C) increased stem length and thickness, as well as the number of xylem vessels.
note: Growth response to a day/night temperature regime against a control regime; the paper reads it through gibberellin and auxin synthesis, and this record logs only the morphological endpoint. Names: POWO page powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:316947-2 lists Solanum lycopersicum L. as accepted; WFO page wfoplantlist.org/taxon/wfo-0001029216-2021-12 lists Solanum lycopersicum as accepted (page flags an older snapshot). Licence sentence read on the publisher PDF: 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).'
